Grey petrel (Procellaria cinerea) chicks hatch from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] and emerge at approximately 60 days [ab = approximately 60 days], a developmental period that falls within the typical range reported for large procellariiform seabirds. Newly hatched nestlings weigh roughly 80 grams [Wwb = roughly 80 grams], a value derived from comparative data for the congener Pterodroma hypoleuca, though direct measurements for this species remain limited. This modest neonatal mass reflects the substantial yolk reserves invested by the parents during incubation. The altricial chick then enters a prolonged nestling phase during which it is brooded and provisioned by both adults, gradually accumulating the body mass necessary for fledging and eventual independence. The thermal environment of the burrow is critical during early development, as it buffers the chick from the cold subantarctic conditions typical of the species' breeding islands.

Under the sustained thermal conditions characteristic of active metabolic periods, approximately 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the nestling grows steadily toward its asymptotic mass, with the ultimate adult wet weight recorded at 1020 grams [Wwi = 1020 grams] for a fully developed individual. This substantial adult body mass, comparable to that of other large Procellaria species, is attained through a diet of fish and squid delivered by the parents during nightly provisioning visits. The fledging process, which marks the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest, occurs at 157 days since birth [tx = 157 days since birth] when maintained at 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This extended nestling period is among the longest recorded for procellariids of similar size, reflecting the high energetic demands of growth in a cold, nutrient-poor marine environment.

In the context of the species' core body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the onset of reproductive maturity occurs after a prolonged juvenile phase. Puberty, defined by the initiation of gonadal activity and the development of mature gametes, is reached at 471 days since birth [tp = 471 days since birth] at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This relatively late maturation, typical of long-lived seabirds, allows individuals to accumulate sufficient body reserves and foraging experience before committing to the energetic demands of reproduction. The intervening juvenile period is spent largely at sea, where young birds hone their hunting skills across the Southern Ocean. During this time, they gradually transition from the post-fledging stage to full adult plumage and physiological competence. The extended pre-reproductive phase is a life-history strategy associated with low annual mortality and high adult survival, traits that characterize the genus Procellaria and enable sustained population persistence despite low reproductive output.

The annual reproductive output of the Grey petrel is notably constrained. Females produce a single egg per breeding attempt [N_R_i = single egg per breeding attempt], and most pairs raise only one brood per year [F_R_i = one brood per year], a pattern consistent with the slow life-history pace of large petrels. This annual reproductive output, reflecting the combined limitation of a single-egg clutch and a single annual breeding event, is among the lowest recorded for procellariiform seabirds. First reproduction in the wild typically occurs at 730 days since birth [tR = 730 days since birth] when maintained at 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], marking the onset of a breeding career that may span several decades. Delaying first breeding beyond the age of gonadal maturity is thought to be adaptive in this species, as younger, less experienced individuals are less likely to successfully fledge a chick on their initial attempt.

Maximum longevity in the Grey petrel is considerable, with the oldest documented individuals reaching approximately 9125 days [am = approximately 9125 days] under natural conditions when core body temperature is maintained at 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This extended lifespan, exceeding those of many smaller procellariids, is consistent with the species' low annual adult mortality and its position as a long-lived, K-selected seabird inhabiting a stable but resource-poor environment. Such longevity allows for repeated breeding attempts across a long reproductive window, partially compensating for the extremely low annual fecundity. The combination of late maturation, single-egg clutches, and extended lifespan forms a coherent life-history syndrome that enables the Grey petrel to persist in the face of stochastic oceanographic conditions and episodic food shortages characteristic of its subantarctic foraging grounds. This suite of traits underscores the importance of adult survival for population stability in this species.
